Hi all, I have a downstream Lean development using Physlib where the complete application is an odd-dimensional average-distance inversion theorem.

The final theorem is:

theorem averageDistance_eq_odd_lintegral_of_boundedContinuous_nnreal
    (m : ℕ)
    (μ ν : Measure (OddSpace m))
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] [IsProbabilityMeasure ν]
    (havg : ∀ y : OddSpace m, averageDistance μ y = averageDistance ν y)
    (g : BoundedContinuousFunction (OddSpace m) NNReal) :
    ∫⁻ x, (g x : ENNReal) ∂μ = ∫⁻ x, (g x : ENNReal) ∂ν

Here OddSpace m is RealEuclideanSpace (2 * m + 1).

The reusable analytic core seems more directly Physlib-shaped: in dimension 2 * m + 1, the (m + 1)-fold distributional Laplacian of the distribution induced by x ↦ ‖x‖ is a nonzero constant times δ₀.

The proof builds on existing Physlib norm-distribution results, especially Space.distGrad_distOfFunction_norm_zpow and Space.distDiv_inv_pow_eq_dim, plus the recurrence
Δ(r^a) = a * (a + d - 2) * r^(a - 2) and iteration to the singular boundary exponent.

I also have a complex tempered-distribution/Fourier version downstream, used in the Cramer-Wold proof, but I suspect the real Space distributional fundamental-solution theorem is the natural part to upstream first.

Questions:

  1. Does this sound suitable for Physlib?
  2. Preferred location: extend SpaceAndTime/Space/Norm.lean, add SpaceAndTime/Space/FundamentalSolution.lean, or something else?
  3. Would you prefer small PRs: first distLaplacian := Space.distDiv.comp Space.distGrad, then the norm-power recurrence, then the odd-dimensional theorem?
  4. Should the main theorem expose the exact constant, or is an ∃ c, c ≠ 0 ∧ ... statement acceptable?

Hi Lazar.

  1. Yes it does! This seems very useful.
  2. Extended SpaceAndTime/Space/Norm.lean sounds good. Not so sure about SpaceAndTime/Space/FundamentalSolution.lean, but this seems a good place to start.
  3. Yes small PRS are very much preferred - and will mean things happen much more quickly.
  4. If it is not so much work to expose exact constants, then I think this is usually better. But an extensional statement is also ok.
Just a note that I added distLaplacian yesterday in Physlib#1138, I realised I should've made it a linear map as well and will fix that tonight
Opps sorry - my brain isn't together right now :).
Thanks a lot for the help, I will start working on the PR(s)!

@Joseph Tooby-Smith, would you be okay with adding me as an outside collaborator on the project? I would prefer to make a PR through my own branch instead of having a fork. I think it would be a better option for the long term, as I plan to make further contributions in the future ;).

Hi Lazar, historically we would have done this - but following Mathlib we converted to forks-only a while back (there is some added security risk with branches). I don't think there is actually much difference between the two approaches. I nowadays use my own fork (here), and it hasn't effected my workflow really at all compared to using branches.
Sure, no problem, thanks a lot!

Just asking out of ignorance, is this just general results regarding distributions or are there specific applications in physics? I'm asking because I've been looking at this area trying to think how to state Poisson's equation and greenfunctions in the context of electrostatics, but the results here seems somewhat orthogonal to that so I'm curious.

Yeah, good question. My direct motivation is not electrostatics, it is the odd-dimensional average-distance / Cramer-Wold inversion theorem.

But the analytic part is basically about Green-function type identities. The final thing I need is
Δ^(m+1) ‖x‖ = c δ₀
in dimension 2 * m + 1, so that is more like a fundamental solution for an iterated Laplacian / polyharmonic operator, not Poisson’s equation directly.

The link to Poisson is the boundary step in the proof: in dimension n, one reaches the usual kind of identity
Δ(r^(2-n)) = c δ₀
for n ≠ 2, using distDiv_inv_pow_eq_dim. So while my downstream theorem is probabilistic, the reusable core is radial distribution calculus around Laplacians and fundamental solutions.

So I think it is not orthogonal to electrostatic Green functions, just a bit more general / differently packaged.

Hi, I'm checking out the new changes, and I'm finding the statements quite confusing. I'm aware the API is built around d.succ, which stems from handling the volume measure of sphere from the Space.Integrals.Basic file. Personally I'd rather d always be the dimension of Space we're working in, and ideally we never have d.succ. We probably need to carry 1 ≤ d or 0 < d around (whichever is more convenient), but is this really worse than what we have now? curious about everyone's thoughts

The good thing about using e.g. d.succ is that for specific values and in simp calls you don’t need to provide the proof (e.g. 3=2.succ by definition). I agree though using d is confusing. I had used dm1 in the past - but I think this is just as confusing. We could do [NeZero d] but doesn’t help for more than one succ

I really think having a separate3 ≤ d is better than d.succ.succ.succ, clarifies what we are working in and the applicability of the lemmas. I'll go through the files and investigate what's the impact and if a better compromise can be made.

I opened a small concrete follow-up PR here: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/pull/1172

It doesn’t try to refactor the broader API yet. It just adds a user-facing wrapper for the newly merged fundamental-solution theorem, stated for Space d with an explicit 3 ≤ d hypothesis and exponent 2 - d, while leaving the existing d.succ.succ.succ theorem as the implementation lemma.

This seems like a lightweight compromise while the larger convention around dimensions is being discussed.

Actually in this case, you don't need the condition that 3 <= d, as you can set the goal up so that it is generally true:

@[simp]
lemma distGrad_const {d} (c : ℝ) : ∇ᵈ (const ℝ (Space d) c) = 0 := by
  ext ε i
  simp only [distGrad_apply, distDeriv_apply]
  simp [fderivD_const]

@[simp]
lemma distLaplacian_const {d : ℕ} (c : ℝ) :
    Δᵈ (const ℝ (Space d) c) = 0 := by
  simp [distLaplacian, distGrad_const]

lemma distLaplacian_fundamentalSolution_norm_zpow_eq {d : ℕ} :
    Δᵈ (distOfFunction (fun x : Space d => ‖x‖ ^ (- ((d - 2 : ℕ) : ℤ))) (IsDistBounded.pow
      _ (by grind))) =(- ((d - 2 : ℕ) : ℝ ) * (d : ℝ) *
        (volume (α := Space d)).real (Metric.ball 0 1)) • diracDelta ℝ 0 := by
  by_cases hd : d < 3
  · have h1 : d - 2 = 0 := by omega
    simp [h1]
    exact distLaplacian_const 1
  · convert distLaplacian_fundamentalSolution_norm_zpow_of_three_le (d := d) (by grind) using 4
    · grind

Thanks, that makes sense. I updated the follow-up PR to use this all-dimensional formulation, with the low-dimensional cases handled by new distGrad_const/distLaplacian_const simp lemmas. The public theorem is now distLaplacian_fundamentalSolution_norm_zpow_eq, while the 3 ≤ d wrapper remains as the bridge to the existing theorem from #1171.
FYI if you put Physlib#1171 instead of #1171 the link goes to the right PR :).

I made Physlib#1183 which removes Space d.succ from everything outside of Norm.lean, I think [NeZero d] or carrying (2 ≤ d) really isn't that bad. If you think this is fine I think I can do the same with the Norm.lean statements as well

That direction makes sense to me. For Physlib#1175, the new iterated-Laplacian statement is already phrased directly over Space (2 * m + 1), so I think it should be compatible with the move away from d.succ.

I’ll keep this PR (Physlib#1175) focused on the odd-dimensional norm Laplacian result and avoid doing the broader Norm API refactor here. If Physlib#1183 or the follow-up Norm refactor is added first, I’m happy to rebase and adjust the proof to the new statements.

Apologies for the delayed follow-up. I meant to ask this earlier, but got pulled into commitments on other projects.

With Physlib#1175 merged, I think the Physlib-side analytic core planned from Physlib#1143 is now complete:

  • Physlib#1143 added the radial norm-power divergence step.
  • Physlib#1169 added the distributional Laplacian recurrence for norm powers.
  • Physlib#1171/Physlib#1172 packaged the fundamental-solution/boundary Laplacian result, including the all-dimensional wrapper.
  • Physlib#1175 added the odd-dimensional iteration theorem with an explicit nonzero coefficient.

So the main reusable statement I needed is now upstream: on Space (2 * m + 1), applying the distributional Laplacian m + 1 times to the distribution induced by ‖x‖ gives oddNormIteratedLaplacianCoeff m • diracDelta ℝ 0, with oddNormIteratedLaplacianCoeff m ≠ 0.

The remaining part of my downstream project is the measure/average-distance inversion application. Roughly, the final theorem says that if two probability measures have the same average-distance function, then they agree on integrals against bounded continuous NNReal-valued test functions.

To finish that downstream, I still need the layer connecting the distributional identity above to the average-distance transform, possibly through a Fourier/tempered-distribution bridge or a more direct measure-theoretic argument.

Before I keep that layer downstream, do maintainers see any reusable part of it that would be useful in Physlib? For example:

  • an existential corollary of the Physlib#1175 theorem;
  • more API around the odd-dimensional coefficient;
  • Fourier/tempered-distribution bridge lemmas;
  • or some average-distance / measure-uniqueness infrastructure.

If that seems too application-specific for Physlib, I’m happy to keep it downstream and only upstream future lemmas if a clearly reusable piece falls out.
I think there is potential for Fourier/tempered-distribution bridge lemmas to be useful here.

That makes sense. Looking at the current API, useful candidates seem to be:

  • injectivity/extensionality lemmas for Distribution.fourierTransform, e.g. u.fourierTransform = v.fourierTransform ↔ u = v and the zero version;
  • a finite-measure-to-tempered-distribution construction/evaluation lemma, together with an extensionality result saying equality of the associated distributions implies equality of finite/probability measures;
  • only after that, a more application-specific lemma connecting the average-distance potential y ↦ ∫ x, ‖x - y‖ ∂μ to the measure distribution via the odd-dimensional iterated Laplacian.

Would a small PR focused first on Fourier-transform injectivity/extensionality for distributions be useful, or would the finite-measure distribution bridge be the better next contribution?
I think the finite-measure-to-tempered-distribution would be nice here, and potentially useful in applications.
I believe the vector measure API in mathlib is being actively developed by @Sébastien Gouëzel , might be worth paying attention to
